case.case_title: Sumanadasa and 205 Others vs. Attorney General
case.source_citation: Sri Lanka Law Reports (2006) 3 Sri L. R. SC SPL 1-199-200-206, decided on 19 June 2006

clause.text: Any person detained shall be brought before a judge and cannot be held without legal order.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioners' continued detention without a procedure established by law to adjudicate their detention violated Article 13(2) of the Constitution.
case_context.petitioner_claim: Petitioners claimed infringement of Article 13(2) due to continuous detention without any recourse to a remedy or procedure established by law to adjudicate their continued detention.
case_context.respondent_argument: Respondent argued that Section 47(1) of the Immigration and Emigration Act, which bars bail for certain offences, is valid existing law and that the petitioners are detained lawfully under this provision.
key_facts: Petitioners were detained under orders of remand by Magistrates for offences under Section 45 of the Immigration and Emigration Act.
Section 47(1) of the Act declares such offences non-bailable and bars release on bail.
Petitioners filed bail applications in the Court of Appeal which were dismissed.
The Divisional Bench had held that no remedy exists for accused persons under Section 47(1) until trial conclusion.
Petitioners were produced before Magistrates but detained without adjudication on continued detention.
The Court found no procedure established by law to adjudicate continued detention as required by Article 13(2).

reasoning.interpretation_summary: Article 13(2) guarantees that any person detained must be brought before a judge according to procedure established by law and cannot be further detained except upon an order made in accordance with such procedure. The Court held that the procedure must include adjudication of continued detention by a competent court.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that Section 47(1) of the Immigration and Emigration Act bars bail and results in indefinite detention without a procedure to adjudicate continued detention, violating Article 13(2). The Court directed that continued detention must be decided according to procedures applicable to non-bailable offences under the Code of Criminal Procedure.
principles_established: The right to be brought before a judge and not detained without legal order includes a right to a procedure to adjudicate continued detention.
Legislative provisions that bar bail without providing a procedure for adjudicating continued detention violate Article 13(2).
The Court has a duty to protect fundamental rights and ensure procedures comply with constitutional guarantees.
precedents_cited: Tunnaya alias Gunapala vs. O.I.C. Galewela

outcome.holding: The Court held that the fundamental rights of the petitioners under Article 13(2) were infringed by their continued detention without a procedure established by law to adjudicate such detention. The Magistrate Courts were directed to decide continued detention according to procedures applicable to non-bailable offences.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Magistrate Courts directed to adjudicate continued detention in accordance with procedure applicable to non-bailable offences; judgment copies to be sent to relevant Magistrate Courts.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(2) was central to the Court's reasoning and holding that the petitioners' indefinite detention without a procedure to adjudicate continued detention violated their fundamental rights, leading to the remedy ordered.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The provision guarantees ... the right not to be further held in custody, detained or deprived personal liberty except upon and in terms of an order of such judge made in accordance with procedure established by law. The Court held that the continued detention without such procedure violates Article 13(2).
